$MMTLP Oh FFS. Now that the MTZZ token theory has been dismantled (see the post below), another theory has emerged that another token was used to “front run” TRCH shares. I don’t even know what the people postulating this theory think that this means, but yet again, the claim that this token has anything to do with TRCH is false. Here’s why:

After looking into the thread and the images being shared, I tracked down this coin too. The screenshots are of TRX transfers on the TRON blockchain, along with one image that’s being called a “white paper” (it’s NOT) for a blockchain currency supposedly used to front-run or short TRCH stock.

These claims do not hold up (again) once you look at the actual public records. Let’s lay out the facts clearly:

Again, the image labeled as the “white paper” is not a white paper at all. It is a standard MIT License text pulled from https://t.co/cajS2qTe88 / GitHub. That file has nothing to do with TRON, TRX, stocks, shorting, or any securities. TRON’s actual whitepapers are publicly available on https://t.co/dslNgEePIo (versions 2.0 and 2.1). They are technical documents about a decentralized content and DApp platform. They contain zero references to TRCH, Torchlight Energy, oil & gas stocks, short selling, or any traditional equities. You can read them yourself.

Second, the blockchain explorer screenshots showing large TRX movements (the “issuance of trx” claims) are normal, public activity on the TRON network. TRON’s total supply started at ~100 billion TRX. Large transfers between foundation addresses, exchange hot wallets, and burns have happened routinely since launch. All verifiable on TronScan. They do not represent some secret issuance tied to stock manipulation. 

Blockchains are transparent by design… if something was being used to conceal activity, it would be one of the worst possible tools for that purpose.

Third, the timelines make any connection impossible. TRON mainnet launched in May/June 2018. TRCH (Torchlight Energy Resources) was a small oil & gas exploration company. The rev merger with Meta… was in June 2021, 3 fuggin years later. TRCH had no crypto token (that I’ve found anyway), no blockchain project, and no involvement with TRON or TRX.

To get more technical… there is also no mechanism for a Layer-1 token like TRX to “front run” or short a stock. Wtf 🤦‍♂️. That is NOT why possible tokenization of TRCH would be of interest to us. Shorting shares happens in equity markets through borrowing and selling on exchanges. Token transfers on TRON are unrelated on-chain activity. 

Real tokenized securities that actually represent stock obligations require legal structures, custody arrangements, disclosures, and regulatory compliance. An anonymous or routine blockchain transfer does not and cannot do that.
TRON itself is a well documented public blockchain focused on scalability, stablecoin transfers (especially USDT), and DeFi.

There is also a separate Nasdaq-listed company (Tron Inc., formerly SRM) that holds TRX as treasury… completely unrelated to TRCH or any energy stock. No records, filings, investigations, or on-chain links connect TRON/TRX to TRCH in any way.

The public data is clear and easy to check:
TRON whitepapers → https://t.co/dslNgEePIo
TRON explorer activity → TronScan

Claims that TRX was issued or used to front-run or short TRCH are not supported by any evidence. They appear to come from misreading routine blockchain screenshots and mislabeling unrelated files. Blockchains make concealment harder, not easier, because everything is public and timestamped. Mama K needs to stop making unsupported and grandiose claims. 

I say again, correcting inaccurate information isn’t an attack on anyone sharing it… it’s necessary so serious discussions with serious people aren’t undermined by claims that fall apart under basic research. The facts here are straightforward and publicly available for anyone to confirm. 

This token has nothing to do with us. AGAIN.

Hasn’t the US already outspent China on AI by a factor of 10? China recently announced $295B capex fund over 5 years, which is less than half of what the US spends in 2026. It’s prob more in PPP terms but US AI capex is clearly not constrained by the short-sightedness of financial media panicking. 

AI buildout in the US, if it's been constrained at all, it's certainly not by the formidable cost or investor and media pressure, but by the physical limitations of power, land and groundswell resistance. Fundamentally, this speaks to America’s limited AI supply elasticity, esp when trying to do so much in a hurry. 

Therein lies the problem. The US has a supply elasticity problem. Most of the hardware (chips, memory, networking) is imported by ally countries also with limited supply elasticities. Domestic grid is dilapidated and ramping up power generation has been a struggle. 

And the inflation pressure that ensues from AI capex also speaks to supply elasticity as AI competes with other use cases over the same input. Inflation also in turn worsens groundswell local opposition. 

China on the other hand has ample supply elasticity, which has become a signature strength due to the extensive, deep and flexible domestic supply chain. It also has the world’s most advanced ultra high voltage electrical grid network. Power isn’t a constraint for China. China’s constraint is advanced GPUs and EUV machines that have been embargoed. 

China has also been further constrained by the fact that AI is just a super expensive and speculative bet with unknown or highly uncertain ROI. If we leave aside govt's push to build out China's own chip industry that started much earlier, China's AI effort so far has been mostly private sector driven.

China's risk capital and investors have lower risk tolerance than their American counterparts and don't want to commit capital to projects without clear path to ROI. Until recently, China incl its tech firms have been watching the US aggressive push into AI somewhat skeptically even as it makes its own push following the US's footsteps in typical fashion. 

So I think this idea of AI as a capex arms race, which attractively maps to the US-USSR Cold War competition, is invalid for the present context. The US and China are running very different races with different conditions. The fact that China is keeping up while doing almost the same things much more efficiently and cheaply seems to be driving folks here a little mad. Always better to run your own race.

As a PhD student, I was told not to work on deep RL - too full of hacks and alchemy" But after a year or two of working in this area, I’ve come to (deeply?) appreciate all of the thoughtful research that’s gone into understanding what/why things work and how to make them better.

My lab (joint with @abhishekunique7) took what we’ve learned by reading this body of literature to answer the question: what are the actual best-practices for finetuning a diffusion/flow/generative robot policy (for now, in sim)? Under one set of constraints - ample compute but limited time on your robot - @servo97  paper gives a pretty compelling answer.
